title: Hub of a Star Network
statement:
A network has n machines labeled 1 to n and is wired as a star: one hub machine is cabled directly to every other machine, and there are no other cables. That is n − 1 cables in total.

You get the cables as edges, where edges[i] = [u, v] means machines u and v are connected. The cables come in any order and either end can be listed first. Return the label of the hub.

examples.why: Machine 3 appears in every cable; each other machine appears once.
With three machines, the hub is the one both cables share. It can be the second entry of a pair.
The first two cables already share only machine 4, which settles it.

constraints: The edges always form a valid star
hints: How many cables touch the hub? How many touch any other machine?
Counting how often each label appears works. But do you need to look at all the cables?
Every cable contains the hub. So any two cables share exactly one machine, and that machine is the hub.

explain.intuition:
In a star, the hub is on every cable and every other machine is on exactly one. A degree count finds it in one pass, which is the general tool for questions like "which node is special".

The star shape allows a shortcut. Take the first two cables. They both contain the hub, and they cannot share any other machine, because a leaf has only one cable. So whichever label appears in both of them is the hub. That is O(1) work no matter how big the network is.
steps: Let the first cable be [a, b] and the second be [c, d].
pitfalls: Assuming the hub is always the first entry of each pair. The ends come in either order.
Assuming the hub has the smallest or largest label.
Building a full adjacency list when a degree count, or just two edges, is enough.

solutions.title: Count degrees
solutions.idea: Count how many cables each machine is on. The hub is on n − 1 of them.

solutions.title: Shared label of the first two cables
solutions.idea: Every cable contains the hub and no leaf is on two cables, so the label common to any two cables is the hub.

followups: The input might not be a star. Check whether it is, in O(n).
The graph is a tree. Find the node whose removal leaves the smallest largest piece (the centroid).
